trial_name: PRORATA — Use of Procalcitonin to Reduce Antibiotic Exposure in ICU (2010)
citation: Bouadma L, Luyt C-E, Tubach F, et al. Use of procalcitonin to reduce patients' exposure to antibiotics in intensive care units (PRORATA trial): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010;375(9713):463-474.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, open-label, superiority/non-inferiority
one_liner: A daily procalcitonin-guided algorithm significantly reduced antibiotic exposure in ICU patients with suspected bacterial infection, though 60-day mortality confidence intervals permitted harm up to 9.7%.

pico.population: Critically ill adults in 7 French ICUs with suspected bacterial infection prompting systemic antibiotics and expected ICU stay >3 days.
pico.intervention: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic algorithm with daily testing and defined initiation/discontinuation cutoffs.
pico.comparison: Standard-care antibiotic management based on contemporary guidelines without clinician access to procalcitonin levels.
pico.outcome: Co-primary: Days without antibiotics (days 1–28, superiority) and all-cause mortality at days 28 and 60 (non-inferiority margin 10%).

background.existing_knowledge: ICU patients experience high empiric antibiotic exposure, driving resistance, drug toxicity, C. difficile infections, and MDRO selection. Clinical signs, radiology, and routine biomarkers like CRP lack specificity for antibiotic discontinuation.
background.knowledge_gap: Prior evidence for procalcitonin-guided stewardship in ICU settings was limited by small trials, heterogeneous protocols, and uncertainty regarding mortality safety.
background.hypothesis: A procalcitonin-guided strategy reduces antibiotic exposure (increasing antibiotic-free days) while remaining non-inferior for 28-day and 60-day mortality compared to standard care.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, open-label trial with stratified allocation by center and variable block size; blinded expert adjudication of infectious outcomes.
methods.setting: 7 adult ICUs in France; patients enrolled at admission or during stay at suspicion of a new bacterial infection.

inclusion: Suspected bacterial infection prompting consideration of systemic antibiotics
exclusion: Receipt of systemic antibiotics for > 24 hours before eligibility assessment
Anticipated need for long-term antibiotic therapy

methods.intervention: PCT-guided strategy: Daily PCT measured at suspected infection up to day 28; results provided within ~2 hours. Initiation guidance at suspicion: <0.25 ug/L strongly discouraged, 0.25 to <0.5 discouraged, 0.5 to <1 encouraged, >=1 strongly encouraged. Discontinuation guidance during therapy: stop strongly encouraged if PCT <0.25 or drop >=80% from peak; stop encouraged if PCT 0.25 to <0.5; continue encouraged if PCT >=0.5 with drop <80%; change antibiotics strongly encouraged if PCT increased vs peak and remained >=0.5. Clinical override was permitted for high-risk syndromes (e.g., septic shock, meningitis) or clinical instability.
methods.comparison: Standard-care antibiotic management based on guidelines and clinician judgement, with PCT values withheld from treating clinicians.
methods.blinding: Open-label for treating clinicians and patients; blinded expert committee adjudicated relapse, superinfection, and confirmed infection.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned sample size 630. Powered for: (1) 133/group for 3-day increase in antibiotic-free days (assumed mean 12, SD 7.5; 90% power, alpha 0.05); (2) 300/group to exclude 10% absolute mortality difference (assumed mortality 35%; 80% power, 10% alpha, two-sided 90% CI). Primary analysis was ITT.
methods.primary_outcome: Co-primary: Days without antibiotics through day 28 (superiority) and all-cause mortality at day 28 and day 60 (non-inferiority margin 10%).
secondary_outcomes: Total antibiotic exposure (days of therapy, day 1-28)
Days of antibiotic exposure per 1000 inpatient days
Duration of first antibiotic episode overall and by syndrome
ICU length of stay from inclusion
methods.follow_up: Antibiotic exposure and clinical outcomes through day 28; mortality assessed at day 28 and day 60.

headline_bullets: PCT guidance increased antibiotic-free days by 2.7 days and decreased total antibiotic exposure by 3.0 days.
Day 28 mortality was nearly identical (21.2% vs 20.4%), but day 60 mortality upper 90% CI reached 9.7%, close to the 10% non-inferiority margin.
No significant differences were seen in relapses, superinfections, MDR acquisition, or ICU length of stay.
Algorithm overrides occurred in 45% of episodes across both groups, highlighting real-world clinician decision-making.

outcomes_table.note: Non-inferiority margin 10%; upper CI allowed harm up to 9.7%

outcomes_table.outcome: Days of antibiotic exposure per 1000 inpatient days

outcomes_table.note: Driven primarily by earlier discontinuation decisions

outcomes_table.outcome: ICU length of stay from inclusion

subgroup_table.subgroup: Duration of first episode: Ventilator-associated pneumonia

safety: Relapse rate through day 28: 6.5% PCT vs 5.1% control (P=0.45)
Superinfection rate through day 28: 34.5% PCT vs 30.9% control (P=0.29)
MDR bacteria acquisition: 17.9% PCT vs 16.6% control (P=0.67)
Day 60 mortality numerically higher in PCT group (30.0% vs 26.1%; 90% CI -2.1% to 9.7%)
Day 28 SOFA score significantly higher in PCT group (1.5 vs 0.9; P=0.0370)

domains.notes: Computer-generated sequence, stratified by center with variable block sizes; allocation concealed prior to assignment.

Open-label design created performance bias potential for antibiotic stopping decisions; objective primary mortality and blinded expert adjudication for relapse/superinfection minimized detection bias.
630 randomised; 9 excluded; 621 in primary ITT analysis (307 PCT vs 314 control). 1 patient per group lost to follow-up at day 60.
Non-adherence occurred in 45% of overall episodes. PCT group had 219 non-adherent episodes (e.g., initiation at PCT <0.5 in 65 cases, delayed stopping); control group had 146 non-adherent episodes.
Well balanced: age 64.4 vs 64.7 years, SAPS II 44.7 vs 42.6, baseline SOFA 7.5 vs 7.2, septic shock 21.8% vs 18.5%, mechanical ventilation 78.5% vs 74.8%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to open-label design and frequent protocol overrides, though core outcomes were objectively measured or adjudicated.

domains.notes: Representative general ICU cohort, but excluded very high severity (SAPS II >65), immunocompromised patients (AIDS, bone marrow transplant), and short-stay patients (<3 days).
7 French ICUs; applicability relies on availability of rapid PCT turnaround (~2 hours) and local baseline antibiotic prescribing habits.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate, applying to general ICU populations with access to rapid PCT assays, but limited in immunocompromised and extremely high-severity cohorts.

strengths: Pragmatic RCT incorporating real-world clinical discretion and overrides into decision support
Co-primary endpoint design explicitly pairing stewardship efficacy with mortality safety
Blinded expert committee adjudication of infectious relapses and superinfections
Rapid PCT assay turnaround (~2 hours) successfully integrated into daily ICU workflow
limitations: Open-label design vulnerable to behavioral prescribing biases and co-intervention differences
High protocol override rate (45%) obscures pure biological algorithm efficacy
Wide 10% non-inferiority mortality margin with day 60 upper CI approaching 9.7%
Single-country trial in 7 French ICUs where control arm treatment durations may differ from global practice

critical_appraisal.summary: PRORATA demonstrates that daily PCT monitoring can successfully drive earlier antibiotic discontinuation in general ICU patients, but high override rates and non-inferiority margin limits necessitate clinical oversight.
strengths: Pragmatic multicenter design with real-world applicability
Blinded expert adjudication of secondary infection endpoints
Clear reduction in overall antibiotic exposure (-3.0 days)
weaknesses: Open-label design subject to performance bias
Permissive 10% non-inferiority margin with day 60 upper 90% CI reaching 9.7%

sections.authors_conclusion: A procalcitonin-guided strategy significantly reduced antibiotic exposure in ICU patients without increasing mortality or infectious complications under a pre-specified 10% non-inferiority margin.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Use daily PCT values as an 'off-ramp' tool to shorten antibiotic treatment duration rather than a trigger to withhold initial empiric treatment.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: General adult ICU patients with suspected bacterial infections (pulmonary, urinary, abdominal) expected to remain in the ICU >3 days.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: PCT should not be used to delay or withhold empiric antibiotics in unstable patients or those with septic shock.
implementation_caveats: Requires rapid PCT turnaround time (~2 hours) to influence daily rounds decisions
Prescribing reductions depend on clinician willingness to stop therapy when PCT drops >=80% or falls <0.25–0.5 ug/L
Not validated in severe immunocompromise (AIDS, bone marrow transplant) or SAPS II >65

controversies.notes: A 10% absolute mortality margin is clinically permissive. Day 60 mortality was numerically higher in PCT group (30.0% vs 26.1%) with upper 90% CI reaching 9.7%.
Clinicians overridden algorithm advice in 45% of episodes, reflecting that PCT functioned as non-binding decision support rather than a strict rule.

context_related_trials.relation: Larger subsequent multicenter ICU trial validating PCT-guided antibiotic duration reduction without excess mortality.

unresolved_questions: Safety and efficacy of PCT algorithms in immunocompromised patients and SAPS II >65 cohorts
Impact of PCT-guided stewardship on long-term institutional antimicrobial resistance rates
Optimal non-inferiority mortality margins for biomarker stewardship trials

numbers_to_remember: Total antibiotic duration: 10.3 vs 13.3 days (-3.0 days, P<0.0001)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Daily PCT monitoring safely reduces ICU antibiotic exposure by ~3 days primarily as a discontinuation signal, but must supplement clinical judgement.
